n: This final chapter is a historical appendix, nearly identical to 2 Kings 24:18–25:30. It confirms that Jeremiah’s prophecies came true. Zedekiah became king at 21 and reigned eleven years (597–586 BC). His mother was also the mother of King Jehoahaz.

f.w: Zedekiah was one and twenty years old

f.g: Not the prophet, who was from Anathoth.

n: Zedekiah did evil in the Lord’s eyes, just as his brother Jehoiakim had.

f.w: according to all that Jehoiakim had done

n: Because of the Lord’s anger, things in Judah reached the point where he cast them out of his presence—and Zedekiah rebelled against Babylon, breaking his oath of loyalty. This was the trigger for the final siege.

f.w: Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon

n: On the tenth day of the tenth month of Zedekiah’s ninth year, Nebuchadnezzar arrived with his whole army, camped around Jerusalem, and built siege works.

f.w: in the tenth day of the month

f.g: Siege walls or towers built around the city.

n: The siege lasted until Zedekiah’s eleventh year—about a year and a half.
By the ninth day of the fourth month, famine was so severe there was no food left for the people. Lamentations describes the horror of these days.

f.w: the famine was sore in the city

n: The wall was breached. The soldiers fled by night through the gate between the two walls near the king’s garden, slipping past the encircling Babylonians toward the Jordan Valley.

f.w: the gate between the two walls

n: The Babylonians chased and caught Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho; his army scattered.

f.w: all his army was scattered from him

n: They took him to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah in Syria, who passed sentence on him.

f.w: Riblah in the land of Hamath

n: Nebuchadnezzar killed Zedekiah’s sons before his eyes, and all Judah’s officials at Riblah. The Book of Mormon tells that one son, Mulek, escaped and was brought to the promised land.
Then he blinded Zedekiah, bound him in bronze chains, took him to Babylon, and imprisoned him until he died. Had he followed Jeremiah’s counsel to surrender, it could have been different.

f.w: put out the eyes of Zedekiah

n: On the tenth day of the fifth month in Nebuchadnezzar’s nineteenth year (586 BC), Nebuzaradan, commander of the guard, came to Jerusalem. (2 Kings gives the seventh day.) Jews mourn the temple’s destruction on the ninth of this month, Tisha B’Av.

f.w: in the fifth month, in the tenth day of the month

n: He burned the Lord’s temple, the royal palace, and all Jerusalem’s houses, including the homes of the leading families. Solomon’s temple, about four centuries old, was gone—as Jeremiah had warned in his temple sermon.

f.w: burned the house of the LORD

n: The Babylonian army tore down all the walls around Jerusalem, leaving it defenseless. Nehemiah would rebuild them about 140 years later.

f.w: brake down all the walls of Jerusalem

n: Nebuzaradan deported some of the poor, the rest of the people still in the city, the deserters who had gone over to Babylon, and the remaining craftsmen.
But he left some of the poorest people to tend vineyards and farm the land.
The Babylonians broke up the huge bronze pillars, the stands, and the great bronze “sea” from the temple and carried the metal to Babylon. Jeremiah had predicted exactly this.
They also took the bronze pots, shovels, wick-trimmers, sprinkling bowls, dishes, and all the bronze utensils used in temple service.
The commander took the basins, fire pans, bowls, pots, lampstands, dishes, and cups—anything of gold or silver.

f.w: that which was of gold in gold
f.g: Whatever was gold, as gold; whatever was silver, as silver—taken for their metal value.

n: The bronze from the two pillars, the sea, the twelve bronze bulls under it, and the stands Solomon made was beyond weighing—too much to measure.
Each pillar was 18 cubits tall (about 27 feet / 8 meters), 12 cubits around (about 18 feet), hollow, with bronze four fingers thick.

f.g: A cubit was about 18 inches (45 cm), the length of a forearm.

n: Each pillar had a bronze capital five cubits high, decorated with bronze latticework and pomegranates all around. These details remind readers of the glory that was lost.

f.g: Capital—the decorative top of a pillar.
A temple symbol of fruitfulness, also on the high priest’s robe.

n: There were 96 pomegranates on the sides and 100 in all around the latticework.
Nebuzaradan also arrested the top temple leaders: Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the second priest, and the three chief doorkeepers. Seraiah was an ancestor of Ezra the scribe.
From the city he also took an officer over the soldiers, seven royal advisers, the army’s chief scribe who drafted men for service, and sixty prominent citizens.

f.g: Literally “who saw the king’s face”—close advisers. 2 Kings 25:19 says five.

n: Nebuzaradan brought them to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah.
Nebuchadnezzar executed them at Riblah. So Judah went into exile from its own land—the covenant curse of exile fulfilled.

f.w: Thus Judah was carried away captive out of his own land

n: Here is a count of the people Nebuchadnezzar deported: in his seventh year, 3,023 Jews—likely the 597 BC deportation (counted differently in 2 Kings, which lists about 10,000, probably including families or using a different count).
In his eighteenth year (586 BC), 832 people from Jerusalem.
In his twenty-third year (about 582 BC), Nebuzaradan deported 745 more—perhaps a reprisal after Gedaliah’s murder. Total: 4,600 people, probably counting only adult men.

f.w: In the three and twentieth year

n: The book ends with a glimmer of hope. In the 37th year of King Jehoiachin’s captivity (about 561/560 BC), the new Babylonian king Evil-merodach released him from prison and treated him with honor.

f.g: Babylonian Amel-Marduk, “man of Marduk,” Nebuchadnezzar’s son (reigned about 562–560 BC). “Evil” is not an English word here.
An idiom for showing favor, releasing from prison.

n: He spoke kindly to him and gave him a seat of honor above other captive kings in Babylon.

Jehoiachin changed out of his prison clothes and ate regularly at the king’s table for the rest of his life. Babylonian ration tablets found by archaeologists actually list oil allotments for “Yaukin, king of Judah” and his sons.

He received a daily allowance from the king until he died. Jeremiah’s book thus closes not in total darkness: David’s line survives in exile, a quiet sign that God’s promises of restoration and of a righteous Branch were still alive.

f.g: A regular daily allowance of food.

f.w: all the days of his life
